sections.html:
Talbot County sits on Maryland's Eastern Shore, with the Chesapeake Bay along its western side and Easton as the county seat. Roughly 44 percent of its 477 square miles is water, and the Choptank, Miles, Wye and Tred Avon rivers cut deep into the land. That is why so many Talbot properties sit on a creek, a cove or river frontage, and why lenders sometimes ask about the shoreline, the road access and the survey.

The 2020 census counted 37,526 residents. Five towns are incorporated: Easton, Oxford, St. Michaels, Trappe and Queen Anne. Easton is the largest, with 17,101 residents. One school system serves the entire county, which keeps listing details simple.

Town lines drive the bill. A house inside Easton, Oxford, St. Michaels, Trappe or Queen Anne carries a municipal levy in addition to county and state charges, while an unincorporated address owes just the county and state portions.

Your value comes from one place and your bill from another. The state assessments department (SDAT) decides what the house is worth for tax purposes and takes first-round appeals. The county Finance Office mails the bill, takes payment and conducts the yearly lien sale.

Walk in at the Talbot County Courthouse, 11 North Washington Street, Suite 9, Easton, or call 410-770-8020. Online, the self-service portal linked from the county tax information page shows a bill and accepts payment.

An owner who is falling behind can also phone the State Tax Sale Ombudsman at 410-767-4994 to ask about the Homeowner Protection Program, covered below.

Where the house sits sets the rate, since the county charge changes from town to town. Fiscal 2026 figures are below. New rates take effect every July 1, so confirm today's number with the Finance Office or on the tax rates page before telling a buyer what the bill will be.

Work out which town, if any, bills your address too. A buyer comparing two Talbot houses will want the combined rate, not just the county line.

Bills open on July 1, and you can pay with no interest until September 30. From October 1, the county adds interest and penalties of one percent for each month or partial month that the balance stays open.

A house you live in qualifies for a split: half by September 30 and half by December 31. The second half comes with a service charge, which a single full payment by September 30 avoids. That charge tops out at 1.279 percent of what remains unpaid in December.

  • July 1: tax year begins and bills are payable.
  • September 30: last day without interest, and first installment date.
  • October 1: interest and penalties start on what is still owed.
  • December 31: second installment for owner-occupied homes.

Selling in the fall? Ask the Finance Office whether the first half is in and whether a service charge is on the account. Your closing agent will need the exact balance.

sections.h2: How are assessments set, and how do you appeal?
sections.html:
Every property is revalued once in three years, and SDAT mails a Notice of Assessment with the old and new market value. In the 2026 round, Talbot County residential values changed by 18.2 percent. A higher value is spread evenly across three years, but a lower one applies immediately. Tell buyers which phase-in year your house is in, since the bill keeps climbing until the full value is reached.

You have 45 days from the notice date to file an appeal. It then moves through three levels:

  1. Supervisor review: a short informal conversation with an assessor, often about 15 minutes.
  2. Appeals Board: file within 30 days after the supervisor's final notice.
  3. Maryland Tax Court: another 30 days after the board rules.

New owners get extra time. If you buy between January 1 and July 1, the 60-day clock starts at the transfer, after the deed is recorded. The SDAT appeal page walks through each filing.

sections.h2: What happens if taxes go unpaid?
sections.html:
Taxes you do not pay attach to the house as a lien. Tax-Property Article section 14-804 makes state, county and town real property tax a lien from the due date until it is paid, and Talbot sells those liens each late spring at its tax sale.

Owners keep the right to redeem after a lien sale by paying the back taxes and fees. Treat the sale as a warning and not as the end. The debt keeps growing, though, and a title company will insist it be cleared before closing.

Owners with low income can apply to the Homeowner Protection Program. It can hold a home out of tax sale for three years or longer and help with the balance. Reach the State Tax Sale Ombudsman at 410-767-4994 or sdat.taxsale@maryland.gov.

sections.h2: Transfer and recordation taxes when you sell
sections.html:
A Talbot deed carries three charges: county transfer tax, state transfer tax and recordation tax. County code puts the first at 1 percent of the price, with the opening $50,000 exempt. The Clerk of the Circuit Court takes payment before recording the deed.

Recordation runs 1.2 percent here and the state transfer tax 0.5 percent, which together with the county's 1 percent makes 2.7 percent on a deed. First-time Maryland buyers of a principal residence get a lower state rate of 0.25 percent, and the seller pays that. Your contract decides who covers the rest.

Rates move, so get the exact numbers from the title company on your settlement sheet. Any back tax comes out of your proceeds at the table, which lowers what you walk away with.

sections.h2: Selling with taxes owed, or an inherited house
sections.html:
An inherited Talbot house can arrive with a tax bill, a lien and nobody living in it. A sale can still happen. The order of steps helps:

  1. Request a payoff from the Finance Office, service charge included, valid through your intended closing day.
  2. Look up the SDAT record for the assessed value and any appeal still open.
  3. Find out whether a town bills the address as well.
  4. Collect the deed and any survey for the title company.
  5. Ask the title company to total the transfer, recordation and town charges before you accept anything.

A house that needs work, or one with taxes behind, is where a cash as-is sale helps most: no buyer's loan to wait on and no repair list from an inspector. We look at Talbot homes in any condition, and you can say no to the offer. Weigh it against a listing's net after repairs, commission and months of holding costs.

faqs.q: When are property taxes due in Talbot County, Maryland?
faqs.a: Bills open July 1 and are interest-free through September 30. Penalties begin October 1. A home you live in may be paid half by September 30 and half by December 31.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Talbot County property tax?
faqs.a: Pay at the Finance Office inside the courthouse at 11 North Washington Street, Suite 9, Easton, or use the county's online portal. Call 410-770-8020 with questions.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal a Talbot County assessment?
faqs.a: The deadline is 45 days after the date printed on the Notice of Assessment. Buyers who take title between January 1 and July 1 get 60 days after the transfer, once the deed is recorded.

faqs.q: Does Talbot County have a transfer tax?
faqs.a: Yes, at 1 percent of the price with the first $50,000 exempt, collected by the Clerk of the Circuit Court. A state transfer tax and a recordation tax come on top.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Talbot County house that is behind on taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. The lien is settled out of your proceeds at closing. Get a payoff figure from the Finance Office before picking a closing date.
